PHASE 4 · ADVANCED PRIMARY CARE CLINICAL MANAGEMENT

Week 93 — Lesson 117: Dizziness, Vertigo & Syncope

FNP-level goal: Replace the vague word dizziness with a time-, trigger-, and symptom-based syndrome; distinguish peripheral vestibular patterns from possible central neurologic disease; and evaluate syncope for cardiac and hemodynamic danger before offering reassurance or a positional maneuver.

Learning Objectives

  • Classify dizziness into vertigo, presyncope, disequilibrium, and nonspecific lightheadedness using timing, triggers, associated symptoms, and functional effect.
  • Recognize common benign positional vertigo patterns while identifying posterior-circulation stroke and other central neurologic red flags.
  • Perform a safe initial syncope assessment that includes history, orthostatic vital signs when appropriate, ECG, medication review, cardiac risk, and focused neurologic examination.
  • Differentiate true syncope from seizure, mechanical fall, intoxication, hypoglycemia, and psychogenic or nonspecific loss of consciousness patterns without dismissing uncertainty.
  • Create an evidence-informed disposition and follow-up plan that prioritizes emergency transfer for unstable, cardiac, neurologic, bleeding, or high-risk presentations.

Part 1 — Dizziness Is a Symptom Family, Not a Diagnosis

When patients say dizzy, do not start by asking whether the room spins and then stop. Ask what they were doing when it began, whether episodes are triggered or spontaneous, how long they last, whether they can walk, and what accompanies them. Vertigo is an illusion of motion. Presyncope is a sense of impending faint or reduced cerebral perfusion. Disequilibrium is imbalance or unsteadiness, often worse with walking. Nonspecific lightheadedness may reflect many causes, including medication effects, anxiety, dehydration, metabolic conditions, anemia, arrhythmia, infection, and multisensory impairment.

A timing-and-trigger approach is safer than an attempt to force a symptom adjective into a diagnosis. Brief triggered episodes with head movement can fit benign paroxysmal positional vertigo. Continuous acute vestibular symptoms with vomiting and gait difficulty require careful distinction between peripheral vestibular neuritis and central causes such as stroke. Transient spontaneous episodes can be vestibular migraine, arrhythmia, transient ischemia, medication effect, or another condition depending on context.

Part 2 — The Initial Safety Screen

Assess vital signs, glucose when clinically indicated, oxygenation, hydration, appearance, mental status, gait if safe, focal neurologic signs, new headache or neck pain, chest pain, dyspnea, palpitations, bleeding, fever, medication changes, substance use, and pregnancy possibility. New focal weakness, speech or swallowing difficulty, diplopia, vision loss, severe inability to walk, severe headache, new severe neck pain, altered consciousness, persistent central nystagmus pattern, or high vascular risk with an acute vestibular syndrome should raise concern for posterior circulation stroke or another central process. Do not dismiss a possible stroke as vertigo because the patient has nausea.

Urgent emergency evaluation is also appropriate for persistent hypotension, shock, active bleeding, severe anemia symptoms, significant arrhythmia concerns, acute coronary symptoms, severe dehydration with instability, or trauma from collapse. The word dizziness can be the first clue to a cardiac, neurologic, hemorrhagic, or metabolic emergency.

Part 3 — Peripheral Vertigo Patterns and Their Boundaries

Benign paroxysmal positional vertigo often causes brief recurrent spinning triggered by rolling in bed, looking up, bending, or changing head position. Hearing loss or focal neurologic deficits are not typical features. When the history and trained examination support BPPV and red flags are absent, a repositioning maneuver may be appropriate; teach safety, fall precautions, and when to return. Do not perform or prescribe a maneuver without considering neck, vascular, mobility, and diagnostic limitations.

Vestibular neuritis may cause prolonged vertigo, nausea, spontaneous nystagmus, and gait difficulty without primary hearing loss. Labyrinthitis includes hearing symptoms. These diagnoses are clinical patterns, but a patient with severe gait inability, new neurologic findings, high stroke risk, severe headache, or atypical course needs central-cause evaluation. In acute vestibular syndrome, specialized eye-movement testing is only reliable in trained hands and does not replace emergency referral when concern is high.

Part 4 — Syncope: A Perfusion Problem Until Proven Otherwise

Syncope is transient loss of consciousness from global cerebral hypoperfusion, with rapid onset, short duration, and spontaneous complete recovery. It differs from a mechanical fall without loss of consciousness, prolonged postictal confusion after seizure, or persistent intoxication, although real cases can be ambiguous. Ask witnesses what happened before, during, and after the event; whether there was prodrome, standing, heat, pain, dehydration, exertion, supine position, palpitations, chest pain, injury, tongue biting, incontinence, movements, recovery time, and family history of sudden death.

Cardiac syncope can be associated with exertion, occurrence while supine, palpitations, structural heart disease, abnormal ECG, family history of sudden death, or absent prodrome. These features lower the threshold for emergency or cardiology-directed assessment. Vasovagal syncope often has a prodrome and recognizable trigger, but a familiar vasovagal story does not exclude risk if the event caused major injury, recurs, or occurs in a patient with cardiac disease.

Part 5 — Orthostatic and Medication-Related Causes

Orthostatic symptoms can arise from volume loss, autonomic dysfunction, medication effects, anemia, infection, deconditioning, and other causes. Obtain orthostatic vital signs using a consistent method when the patient is stable and this will inform care; do not make a patient with concerning symptoms stand for a measurement. Review antihypertensives, diuretics, alpha-blocking agents, psychoactive medicines, sedatives, diabetes therapies, alcohol, and other substances. Medication review should ask not only what is prescribed, but what was recently started, increased, stopped, borrowed, or used intermittently.

Finding orthostatic hypotension does not end the workup if the history suggests arrhythmia, bleeding, stroke, or other serious cause. It can coexist with cardiac disease, autonomic neuropathy, or medication harm. The plan may include volume and medication management, fall-prevention support, chronic disease assessment, and close follow-up, but only after dangerous causes are reasonably addressed.

Part 6 — Focused Examination and Testing

Examine heart rhythm and murmurs, lungs, volume status, neurologic function, gait, cranial nerves, strength, sensation, coordination, nystagmus when trained, ears when clinically relevant, and signs of trauma or bleeding. Obtain a 12-lead ECG in initial syncope evaluation when available; it can reveal conduction disease, arrhythmia clues, ischemic changes, or inherited-pattern concerns. Tests such as CBC, metabolic studies, pregnancy testing, glucose, troponin, ambulatory rhythm monitoring, echocardiography, or imaging are chosen because history and examination raise a specific question—not as a universal panel for every dizzy patient.

Document the symptom syndrome, timing, triggers, associated symptoms, risk factors, orthostatic or ECG findings, differential, decision rationale, and clear disposition. If you cannot confidently classify the syndrome, that uncertainty itself may justify a safer disposition or consultation.

Part 7 — Avoid Harm From Premature Reassurance

Common errors include diagnosing anxiety before checking vital signs and neurologic status, calling all head-movement dizziness BPPV, attributing collapse to dehydration without an ECG or cardiac history, and assuming older adults fall because of age. Another error is overtesting low-risk recurrent BPPV-like episodes without a targeted examination. FNP-level care avoids both extremes: do not miss danger, and do not turn every benign pattern into unnecessary emergency testing.

Part 8 — FNP Case: Brief Vertigo When Rolling Over

A 54-year-old has 20-second episodes of spinning when rolling in bed or looking upward, with normal gait between episodes, no hearing change, no neurologic symptoms, and a compatible positional examination by a trained clinician. The FNP identifies a likely BPPV pattern, provides or arranges a safe repositioning approach, explains fall precautions, and gives strict return instructions for persistent symptoms, new headache, weakness, vision change, or inability to walk.

Part 9 — FNP Case: Continuous Vertigo and Gait Failure

A 70-year-old with hypertension and diabetes has sudden continuous vertigo, vomiting, new inability to walk unassisted, and diplopia. This is not an office BPPV maneuver visit. The FNP recognizes central neurologic red flags and arranges emergency stroke-capable evaluation. The clinical mistake would be to anchor on the word vertigo.

Part 10 — FNP Case: Collapse During Exercise

A 38-year-old collapses while running, has no clear prodrome, reports recent exertional palpitations, and has a family history of early sudden death. Although they recovered quickly, exertional syncope with cardiac red flags requires urgent cardiac evaluation. The FNP obtains or arranges ECG and emergency assessment according to stability; reassurance based on young age would be unsafe.

FNP High-Yield Framework: STAND

  1. S — Specify the syndrome: vertigo, presyncope, disequilibrium, lightheadedness, or true syncope.
  2. T — Time and triggers: seconds versus hours, positional versus spontaneous, exertional versus supine, and recovery pattern.
  3. A — Assess danger: neurologic deficit, gait failure, chest symptoms, palpitations, hypotension, bleeding, trauma, and high-risk history.
  4. N — Narrow tests to the question: ECG, orthostatics, glucose, labs, imaging, and referral only when clinically indicated.
  5. D — Decide disposition and document: emergency transfer, same-day evaluation, outpatient plan, fall precautions, and follow-up.

Take-Home Summary

Dizziness becomes manageable when it is classified by timing, triggers, and associated symptoms. Syncope becomes safer when it is approached as a perfusion event requiring history, examination, ECG, and risk stratification. The FNP recognizes a benign positional pattern when it is truly present but never allows that recognition to obscure stroke, arrhythmia, hemorrhage, metabolic instability, or medication harm.

Educational note: This lesson supports clinical reasoning and does not replace emergency or neurologic evaluation, cardiology consultation, ECG interpretation expertise, vestibular examination training, or individualized clinical judgment. New focal neurologic symptoms, inability to walk, severe headache or neck pain, chest pain, palpitations with collapse, exertional or supine syncope, active bleeding, persistent hypotension, or trauma requires urgent evaluation.
